source_text: Quare si animam totiens mutabilem siue uariarum uoluntatum turba siue adfectibus pro rerum copia uel inopia sese flectentibus siue ipsis innumerabilibus ludis phantasmatum . siue obliuione et memoria siue doctrina et inperitia: si ergo animam, ut dixi, his atque huiusmodi motionibus totiens mutabilem sentis non diffundi extendique per locos, sed omnia talia spatia potentiae uiuacitate superare, quid de ipso deo cogitandum aut existimandum est. qui supra omnes rationales mentes inconcussus atque incommutabilis manens tribuit, quod cuique tribuendum est? quem facilius eloqui audet anima quam uidere, et quem tanto minus eloquitur, quanto sincerius uidere potuerit. qui tamen, si, ut Manichaeorum phantasmata perstrepunt, locorum ex una parte determinato, ex aliis inmenso spatio tenderetur, quantaelibet in eo particulae et innumerabilia frusta alia maiora, alia minora pro cogitantis arbitrio metirentur, ut bipedalis in eo uerbi gratia pars octo partibus minor esset quam decempedalis. id enim necesse est contingat omnibus naturis, quae per talia spatia diffusae ubique totae esse non possunt, quod in ipsa anima non inuenitur et ab eis, qui haec considerare non ualent, deformiter de illa et turpiter creditur.
thought_title: The soul's power over space shows what God must be
orientation: Augustine is arguing against the Manichaean picture of God as a body spread through space, using the soul's non-spatial power of judgment as a clue to God's nature.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore if you perceive the soul, so often changeable either by a crowd of varying wills or by feelings bending themselves according to plenty or want of things or by the very innumerable plays of fantasies, or by forgetfulness and memory or by teaching and inexperience: if therefore you perceive the soul, as I said, changeable so often by these and motions of this kind, not to be poured out and extended through places, but to surpass all such spaces by the liveliness of its power, what is to be thought or judged about God himself, who remains unshaken and unchangeable above all rational minds, and grants what is to be granted to each? Whom the soul dares to speak out more easily than to see, and whom it speaks out the less, the more sincerely it has been able to see. Who nevertheless, if, as the Manichaeans' fantasies make a din, he were stretched out through space bounded on one side, unbounded in extent on the others, however many little parts in him and innumerable bits, some larger, some smaller, would be measured according to the judgment of the thinker, so that a two-foot part in him, for example, would be smaller by eight parts than a ten-foot part. For this must happen to all natures which, poured out through such spaces, cannot be whole everywhere, which is not found in the soul itself and is believed about it in a deformed and shameful way by those who cannot consider these things.

choices.english: by the liveliness of its power
choices.why: Keeps the genitive relation explicit and renders uiuacitas as liveliness to convey active, non-spatial power.
rejected: by the vigor of its power

choices.why: Preserves the two adjectives as distinct attributes of God and the participial force of manens.
Captures the noisy, insistent character of the Manichaean fantasies that Augustine is mocking.
Renders the concrete, physical fragmentation implied by the Manichaean picture of God as a body.

choices.term: deformiter de illa et turpiter creditur
choices.english: is believed about it in a deformed and shameful way
choices.why: Keeps the two adverbs as parallel modifiers of the believing, preserving Augustine's moral condemnation.
rejected: is believed about it deformedly and basely
is believed of it in an ugly and disgraceful manner

pass_b_english: So if you perceive that the soul, so often changeable—whether through a crowd of shifting wills, or through feelings that bend it this way and that according to the abundance or lack of things, or through the countless games of fantasies, or through forgetfulness and memory, or through learning and inexperience—if, as I said, you perceive that the soul, so often changeable through these and similar motions, is not spread out and extended through places, but surpasses all such spaces by the liveliness of its power, then what must be thought or judged about God himself? He remains unshaken and unchangeable above all rational minds, giving to each what is due to each. The soul dares to speak of him more easily than to see him, and the more purely it is able to see him, the less it speaks of him. Yet if, as the Manichaeans' fantasies make a din, he were stretched out through places—bounded on one side, but of infinite extent on the others—then however many particles and countless bits in him, some larger, some smaller, could be measured at the whim of the one thinking, so that, for example, a two-foot part in him would be eight parts smaller than a ten-foot part. For this must happen to all natures that are spread through such spaces and cannot be wholly everywhere. But this is not found in the soul itself, and it is believed about it in a deformed and shameful way only by those who are unable to consider these things.

last_rejected.quote: it is believed about it in a deformed and shameful way only by those who are unable to consider these things
last_rejected.source_quote: quod in ipsa anima non inuenitur et ab eis, qui haec considerare non ualent, deformiter de illa et turpiter creditur
last_rejected.why: English 'it' refers to soul, but source 'illa' refers to God; last clause is about God, not soul.
last_rejected.fix: But this is not found in the soul itself, and about God it is believed in a deformed and shameful way by those unable to consider these things.
last_rejected.ruling: 'illa' grammatically refers to 'ipsa anima'; the clause contrasts what is not found in the soul with false belief about it.

last_rejected.quote: the Manichaeans' fantasies make a din
last_rejected.why: Glossary bans 'imaginary pictures' and 'mental images' but 'fantasies' is required; however 'phantasmata' here should be 'fantasies' per glossary. Actually checking: 'perstrepunt' = 'make a din/noise'—this is fine. But wait—'phantasmata' = 'fantasies' per glossary. This seems correct.
last_rejected.ruling: Checker confirms 'phantasmata' = 'fantasies' and 'perstrepunt' = 'make a din' are both correct; no error identified.

last_rejected.why: 'Inperitia' means 'ignorance, lack of skill', not 'inexperience' which suggests lack of practice rather than lack of knowledge.
last_rejected.ruling: 'inperitia' includes 'inexperience' within its semantic range; paired with 'doctrina' (learning), the contrast is valid.

last_rejected.quote: however many particles and countless bits in him, some larger, some smaller
last_rejected.source_quote: quantaelibet in eo particulae et innumerabilia frusta alia maiora, alia minora
last_rejected.why: quantaelibet means of whatever size, not however many; number is already in innumerabilia.
last_rejected.fix: particles in him of any size you please, and countless bits, some larger and some smaller, would be measured
last_rejected.ruling: quantaelibet can mean 'however many/any amount of'; 'quantaelibet particulae' (plural) as 'however many particles' is within range, and the sense of measuring parts is preserved.
